12191-the-red-axe:
S. R. Crockett published this historical romance in 1900, set in a fictional German border state of dukes, wolves, and witches. The narrator, Hugo Gottfried, serves as the Red Axe, headsman of the Wolfmark, and tells his own rise and fall.

Hugo loves the princess Helene, serves Duke Casimir, and becomes entangled in treason, witch trials, and a struggle for the throne. Chapters move from the bar of the White Wolf to the red tower, the dungeon of Wolfsberg, and the crowning of Duke Otho. Crockett piles on sword fights, escapes, and revelations with cheerful excess. The novel is pure swashbuckle, best read for pace and color rather than history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-saxe:
Jean de Saxe is a name long shared by two medieval astronomers this entry works to separate. The first, Joannes Danko, also called de Danekowe, wrote notes on the computus, the church calendar reckoning, in 1297, and copied Jean de Linières's canons at Paris in 1323.

The second, Jean de Counnout, also called de Connaught, admired Linières and wrote widely on stars and planets. His canons on King Alfonso's tables, drawn up in 1327, won lasting fame, and his notes on Al-Kabici and his worked examples for Paris students spread through many printings. Untangling the two men clears a long-standing mix-up in astronomy's history.

nasa-tm-19710028802-effect-of-shield-wei:
Millard L Wohl and David Spielberg of the Lewis Research Center wrote this November 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2414. It asks what a fixed containment vessel costs in shield weight for a mobile reactor. The reactors were rated at two hundred fifty megawatts. Their unit shields mixed tungsten and water in rounded layers. The vessel would sit inside the shield as one of its layers.

A computer code computed the best shield weights for three reactor types. The team then added vessels of three wall thicknesses. The added shield weight came out far below the vessel weights themselves. Poor placement of the heavy vessel explained the increase that remained. The result favored building the vessel into the shield.
podcast-joerogan-0eCTMVherxE:
Comedian Tom Segura returns to Joe Rogan for episode 2505. Segura co-hosts the hit show Your Mom's House. His dry, dark style has filled arenas worldwide.

The two old friends trade tales of tours, fame, and family life. Segura shares bits and stories in his flat, sly tone. Rogan knows his act and his life well. The talk feels like a green room chat caught on tape. Fans of either comic get an easy, funny hour with almost no filler and plenty of inside jokes. The laughs land from the first exchange onward.
podcast-joerogan-ERMnvDv2exE:
UFO filmmaker James Fox returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1976, a follow-up to his other visits. Fox builds his documentaries from witness testimony and records, and Rogan treats him as a beat reporter on the disclosure story. Each visit updates the last.

Fox shares the cases and footage he had gathered since his prior appearance, and grades which claims he trusts. Rogan pushes on the strongest stories and the weakest links alike. For listeners tracking the subject over time, the episode works as a dated field report, useful for seeing how the story moved between his visits.
podcast-joerogan-IErO3RuGTXE:
Neuropharmacologist Andrew Gallimore joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2403 to discuss his DMT research. Gallimore studies the drug's effects on the brain and has proposed bold ideas about the worlds users enter. His work sits where chemistry meets reports of other realms.

He explains what DMT does in the brain, why its trips feel so real, and his case for longer, controlled sessions to map the space. Rogan asks the question every listener wants answered: are the beings users meet actually there? The episode is a serious scientist's tour of the strangest drug experience known.
podcast-joerogan-g2AyNRVWOxE:
Quarterback Baker Mayfield's reported UFO sighting gets taken up in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Mayfield said he and his wife saw a strange light drop from the sky while driving in Texas. When a star athlete tells such a tale, Rogan pays attention.

The talk runs through what the couple reported and how the story played in sports media, where jokes came easy. Rogan asks why pilots and players who report sightings risk ridicule to tell them. The segment is a light, short piece of sky-watching, notable for the witness's day job under stadium lights.
podcast-joerogan-lPRTYOJeIxE:
UFO investigators give their account of the David Grusch hearings in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Grusch, the whistleblower, had just testified to Congress that secret programs hold alien craft. The researchers who watched it unfold join Rogan to dissect the moment.

They sort the testimony's strongest claims from its weakest, and grade how lawmakers and reporters handled them. Rogan asks what the hearings changed in law and in public mood. The segment is a close read of the disclosure era's biggest day, by people who had waited decades for a hearing like it.
roughing-it-de-luxe: Irvin S. Cobb wrote Roughing It De Luxe, with pictures by John T. McCutcheon, under copyrights of 1913 and 1914. Cobb is named as the author of Back Home, The Escape of Mr. Trimm, Cobb's Anatomy, and Cobb's Bill of Fare. The book is given to George H. Doran, hailed as both friend and publisher. A time table lists five pieces: A Pilgrim Canonized, Rabid and His Friends, How Do You Like the Climate, In the Haunt of the Native Son, and Looking for Lo.
the-red-axe: S. R. Crockett published his romance in 1900, and its contents run to more than forty chapters around Duke Casimir, Princess Helene, blood-hounds, a white wolf's bar, and a red axe in the Wolfmark. Headings promise traitors, visions in a crystal, emerald eyes, flights, duels, a witch trial, and a garret in a red tower. Here only the title and contents list are present, so the romance itself does not appear.
